summary: EviDAG is a browser-based tool from MGH/Harvard for drafting causal DAGs (the epidemiology kind, not task graphs) from biomedical literature. A fixed staged pipeline resolves study variables (optionally to UMLS), builds a frozen PubMed snapshot per concept pair, has Claude Sonnet 4.6 issue per-pair causal judgments with verbatim cited snippets, and assembles a constraint-checked DAG with confidence, provenance and adjustment sets. On 7 small synthetic and 3 published literature DAGs it has higher recall but lower precision and F1 than simply asking the same model for the whole graph. Unlike that baseline, every citation is verifiable.

claims.claim: EviDAG achieves high edge recall on the literature-based cohort.
claims.evidence: Table 1/4: literature cohort recall 0.87 cold / 0.91 with context vs direct-LLM baseline 0.78 / 0.83. Three reference DAGs only; medians of three temperature-0 runs, baselines single pass. PubMed cutoff set before each source study's publication to prevent retrieving the reference paper.

claims.claim: EviDAG retains verifiable evidence trails absent from LLM-only baselines.
claims.evidence: App. A: 0 of 211 (direct) and 0 of 812 (pairwise) baseline quotes appear verbatim in the cited abstract; EviDAG citations are extracted spans by construction. 116/161 literature-cohort pairs are literature-backed, 45 prior-only.

claims.claim: Implied by the abstract: EviDAG is a better DAG author than LLM-only baselines; it 'reduces the burden of causal DAG curation'.
claims.evidence: Table 4: the same model prompted once for the whole graph has higher directed F1 on the literature cohort (0.78 vs 0.66 cold; 0.80 vs 0.71 with context) and ties on synthetic DAGs (0.89 vs 0.88). The abstract omits this. No user study measures curation burden; §4 lists it as future work.

patterns.note: A fixed staged pipeline (orchestrator, deterministic constraints, review pauses, typed artifacts) is compared with the same model and a single direct prompt. The pipeline wins recall and auditability, loses precision and F1 on literature DAGs, and ties on small DAGs. A pairwise-decomposed baseline (one prompt per pair plus deterministic assembly) is worse than the single prompt (F1 0.70 vs 0.78), so finer decomposition alone hurt. The domain is causal-graph authoring, not coding, and the DAG here is the output artifact, not a task graph.
Per-edge provenance channels, frozen literature snapshot and audit replay; strong on verifiability, no user evaluation.
Configured review pauses before downstream stages; not evaluated.

methodology.sample: 7 synthetic compact DAGs (66 concept pairs) and 3 published literature DAGs (161 pairs).
methodology.baselines: Same model (Claude Sonnet 4.6) prompted directly for the whole DAG, and per-pair with deterministic assembly; no prior LLM-causal-discovery systems.
methodology.variance: Medians of three temperature-0 runs for EviDAG; baselines single pass; no spread reported.
methodology.ablations: Confidence-tier inclusion policies; cold vs study-context input.
methodology.contamination_controls: PubMed cutoff the day before each reference study's publication; model prior knowledge of the published DAGs not controlled.

standards.artifacts: No code or data link found; configuration described in App. A.

biases.detail: Three literature DAGs carry the headline recall claim.
Abstract emphasises recall; F1 and precision, where the plain-prompt baseline wins, are moved to Table 4 discussion.
Abstract claims reduced curation burden with no user evaluation.

coi.affiliations: Massachusetts General Hospital; Harvard University; Northeastern University.
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Claude Sonnet 4.6 used as backbone (no affiliation).
coi.detail: Academic clinical-research authors; no vendor tie.

verdict_reason: Off-topic for this KB. The 'DAG' is a causal graph for epidemiological analysis, not a task or workflow graph, and the system is a literature-curation tool, not a coding-agent harness. The evaluation is also thin (three literature DAGs, one model), and the abstract's framing hides that a single direct prompt beats the pipeline on F1.
applicability: This does not transfer to the DAG-workflow question; the shared word 'DAG' is coincidental. One tangential point for a healthcare-education ingestion team: when an LLM step must cite sources, extracting and verifying verbatim spans against a frozen snapshot made every citation checkable. The unconstrained baselines produced 0 verifiable quotes out of 1,023 and mostly cited the wrong PubMed IDs. That argues for deterministic citation verification in any content-ingestion step that attributes clinical claims, independent of how the workflow is structured.
